title: Strength With Cancer in the Picture
subtitle: For adults 65 and older, a useful starting point is not a generic workout. It is identifying what matters in daily life, then finding the right support to work toward it.
imageAlt: Two friends at a kitchen table review a short list of questions about strength, mobility and exercise support during cancer care.
imageConcept: Two older friends sit together at a bright kitchen table, one holding a notebook while the other points to a question about getting up from a chair. A water glass and reading glasses sit nearby; the mood is collaborative and calm, with no exercise equipment or staged medical scene.
body: Begin with what you want to keep doing

Cancer can make a strength question feel abstract: Should I exercise? How much? Is it safe? A more useful first question is often specific to the person’s life. Is there a walk to the bus stop they want to keep making? A grandchild they hope to lift, a garden they want to tend, or stairs they would like to manage with less effort? These priorities do not prescribe a workout. They give the care team and an exercise or rehabilitation professional a practical starting point for discussing goals, current abilities and appropriate support.

That individualized approach is especially relevant for adults 65 and older living with or beyond cancer. A 2026 expert consensus statement developed recommendations for this group, addressing a gap in guidance rather than offering one standard program for every older adult [1]. Strength work can be part of the conversation, but the person’s circumstances—not an age-based template—should shape it.
Why the starting point deserves attention

Treatment, recovery and living with cancer vary widely. So do mobility, balance, strength, symptoms and other health conditions. Two people with the same cancer diagnosis may have very different capacities and priorities; the same person may also need a different approach at different points in treatment or recovery. That is why a plan that begins with a person’s current function is more useful than one built around a generic list of exercises.

The 2026 consensus was created through expert input, research review and a community advisory board. Its recommendations are consensus guidance, not proof from a large set of trials specifically involving older cancer survivors [1]. That distinction matters: the statement offers a considered framework for care, while leaving room for clinical judgment and the details of an individual’s health. It also complements broader cancer-exercise guidance rather than replacing it.

The consensus recommends that programming for older survivors with significant deficits in strength, mobility or balance address those needs first, and include functional movement patterns [1]. In practice, that points toward assessment before choosing a routine. A qualified professional may ask about tasks that have become harder, observe relevant movements, and consider symptoms and treatment circumstances. The goal is not to grade someone or prove readiness; it is to understand what support and modifications may be appropriate.

A functional focus connects training to everyday tasks: rising from a chair, carrying groceries, reaching for a cupboard or moving safely through the home. These examples are not a prescription to test yourself at home. They are useful prompts for describing what matters and what has changed. If a movement feels unsafe or brings on concerning symptoms, stop and bring that information to the care team rather than trying to push through it.

For people receiving active cancer treatment with curative intent, the American Society of Clinical Oncology guideline recommends aerobic and resistance exercise to help mitigate treatment side effects [2]. The guideline also says evidence was not sufficient to recommend exercise for improved cancer-control outcomes such as recurrence or survival. That is an important boundary: exercise can be discussed as part of supportive care without promising that it will change the course of cancer.

Evidence for resistance training during chemotherapy is also mixed and limited. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis included seven randomized trials with 561 participants. It found evidence of improved lower-body strength, but no clear effect on several other outcomes it assessed, including fatigue, quality of life, physical function and upper-body strength; the authors noted limitations in the evidence [3]. Those results do not mean exercise is useless, or that every individual will have the same response. They do mean that claims should stay modest and plans should be tailored.
Turn a concern into a useful conversation

Before an appointment, write down one or two activities that matter and what makes them difficult now. Be concrete: “I want to manage the steps to my apartment,” or “I am unsure whether I can carry a small grocery bag.” Note when the difficulty occurs and any symptoms or changes you have noticed. You do not need to diagnose the cause. The point is to give the care team information they can use.

Then ask direct questions: Is there anything about my current treatment or health that should shape exercise right now? Would an assessment of strength, balance or mobility help? Is there an exercise oncology, physical therapy or rehabilitation professional you recommend? What symptoms should prompt me to stop and contact the team? The answers may depend on the person’s cancer, treatment and health. A useful appointment can end with a referral, a follow-up question or a clear decision to revisit the topic later.
Choose the right kind of support

The right professional depends on the person’s needs and local options. A physical therapist or rehabilitation clinician may be appropriate when mobility, balance, pain or daily function is a concern. An exercise professional with relevant cancer-care experience may help translate clinical guidance into a feasible program. The cancer-care team can advise on referrals and on how treatment circumstances affect the conversation. The key is not a particular title in isolation; it is a professional who understands the person’s situation and works within their expertise.

The 2026 consensus also emphasizes implementation and support, including social support and involvement from cancer-care teams, caregivers and family [1]. A friend or relative can help by taking notes, arranging transport, or asking what role would be welcome. They should not diagnose, make treatment decisions or pressure someone to exercise. Support is most useful when the person receiving it remains in charge of their goals and choices.
Make a plan that can adapt

If an appropriate professional recommends a program, ask how it can change when energy, symptoms or treatment schedules change. Clarify what movements are intended, how to modify or pause them, and whom to contact with questions. Ask how progress will be assessed: perhaps by whether a meaningful daily task feels more manageable, not by a number on a scale or a comparison with someone else. Write down the agreed plan in plain language, including any limits and the next check-in.

A plan may need to be adjusted over time. That is not failure or lack of commitment; it is part of responding to a changing health context. The older-adult consensus specifically calls attention to functional assessment and symptom monitoring [1]. Those ideas support a flexible process: notice what is happening, communicate with the appropriate professional, and revise the plan when needed rather than treating a written routine as fixed.
A first step that respects the person

Choose one task the person wants to keep doing and ask whether they would like help preparing a conversation with their care team. Write the task in their own words, add one question about assessment or referral, and bring the note to an appointment—or send it through the clinic’s usual communication channel. If a friend or family member is involved, ask what help is wanted: taking notes, finding a professional, or simply listening. Keep exercise decisions with the person and qualified professionals who understand their health and treatment. The aim is not to turn every day into a test of strength. It is to make room for a practical, individualized conversation about function, support and the activities that matter.
